name: Nigerian nationalism
summary: Nigerian nationalism began as the demand to end British rule and, after 1960, became the effort to build one nation out of about 200 ethnic groups under a federal state. It holds the colonial borders fixed, keeps the federation together by force if need be, protects rights across ethnic lines and keeps Nigeria out of the Cold War blocs. It leaves most economic, social and moral questions open.
scope: Ibhawoh's account of Nigerian nationalism: the anticolonial movement (Macaulay, Azikiwe, Awolowo's early period) and the postcolonial integration project, with the Balewa government's speeches (1949-64) as its main primary text and the federal state's record in the civil war. It excludes the regional and ethnic nationalisms Ibhawoh says split the movement before independence (Awolowo's 'mere geographical expression' view, the Northern People's Congress's regional aims, Biafra).

national-self-determination.rationale: Nigerian nationalism began as the demand for self-rule: the Nigerian Youth Movement proclaimed 'immediate and complete independence', and Balewa's 1960 speech calls independence the culmination of that effort and later speeches back the self-determination of other African peoples.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Balewa told the 1960-63 African conferences that, however artificial the colonial boundaries were, it is Nigeria's policy to leave them as they are and discourage any adjustment (Nigeria's Stand; Addis Ababa).

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Balewa accepts that colonial borders cut across peoples but rejects any adjustment, and warns that disregarding them would bring trouble to the continent (Nigeria's Stand; Addis Ababa).

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Balewa recognises all existing African boundaries, drawn by colonial partition, as the basis of African unity, so he does not treat the partition as void.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The Balewa government's stated policy is to discourage any boundary adjustment in Africa, which excludes demanding territory back.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Balewa says Nigeria has 'no aggressive intentions' and recognises all existing boundaries, (Nigeria's Stand; Addis Ababa).

territorial-expansion.rationale: Balewa states Nigeria 'shall never impose ourselves upon any other country' despite its size, and treats every African territory as an equal.

right-to-secede.rationale: The federal state's record is that it fought the 1967-70 Biafra War to keep the country together, and Ibhawoh calls the secession the most serious threat to the Nigerian nation.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The federal government declared an emergency and fought the civil war until Biafra surrendered in 1970 (Ibhawoh), which is the postcolonial state's record, though the war was fought under a military government.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Balewa: 'Nigeria has adopted a policy of non-alignment', refusing to ally with either bloc; the policy was affirmed at Monrovia.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Postcolonial Nigerian nationalism sought a shared national belonging across about 200 ethnic groups, and Balewa made 'unity in diversity' of the 'different tribal communities' the basis of the country.

racial-franchise.rationale: The independence constitution guaranteed basic rights to every Nigerian, and Balewa addressed all Nigerians whatever their religion or status; no office or vote was limited to one group in the nationalist programme.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: After the civil war the federal government's principle was 'No victor, no vanquished' with reintegration of Igbos into the civil service, police and army.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Balewa says 'unity in diversity is a source of great strength', though Ibhawoh records that the country's diversity remains its main challenge.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Balewa describes the independence constitution's chapter three on fundamental rights, entrenched so that changing it needs two-thirds of both houses and two regions; Ibhawoh confirms the Bill of Rights.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Balewa names equality before the law, within states and among states, as an essential ingredient of the rule of law and condemns apartheid and white supremacy.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Balewa condemns South African apartheid and white minority rule in Southern Rhodesia, and Nigeria joined sanctions against South Africa.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The nationalist movement aimed at ending British rule and demanded self-government; Balewa's thanks to British officers does not accept that rule was rightful.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Ibhawoh describes colonial rule as excluding Africans and discriminating against them, and Balewa says colonial trade arrangements sacrificed developing countries' interests.

decide-locally.rationale: Balewa defends federal regional government as the sure basis of unity, while the later nationalist military governments centralised power and created more states, so adherents divide.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Federalism was adopted with regional autonomy partly to protect minority interests, but the 1957 commission rejected more states for minorities and later regimes redrew the states, so the record is mixed.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Independence was arranged so that no ethnic group held all power (a Northern prime minister, an Eastern head of state, a Western opposition leader), and the 1979 federal character principle spreads appointments by region.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Nationalist governments promoted pride in Nigerian culture, local dress for officials abroad and a national anthem about the fatherland, within a framework that keeps ethnic differences.

patriotic-education.rationale: Postcolonial nationalist governments such as Buhari's 1984 campaign made daily anthem recitals compulsory in schools and promoted patriotism, though results were limited.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Balewa's Six-Year Development Plan provides for direct government participation in industry and partnership with foreign investors, though not for a state monopoly.

public-ownership.rationale: Balewa's 1964 statement rejects nationalisation in favour of free enterprise and private capital, while the plan also provides government participation in industry.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Balewa's government welcomes private foreign capital and says it does not seek its withdrawal before Nigerian enterprise can replace it.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Balewa argues that the poor nations' commodity trade is disadvantaged and calls for global action on commodity prices and lower trade barriers for developing countries.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Balewa calls aid a temporary phenomenon and self-reliance the basis of happiness, yet his government sought large loans and aid, so the record is mixed.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Balewa's government accepted the vote of the Southern Cameroons on whether to rejoin Nigeria or join the Cameroon Republic, saying the people's votes decide.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Balewa calls the UN 'the only guarantee of our freedom' for small nations and accepts some curtailment of sovereignty under the rule of law, but refuses a union government for Africa.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Balewa will not voluntarily surrender Nigeria's sovereignty to an African union government now, while not ruling out eventual union as cooperation grows.

non-intervention.rationale: Balewa warns against states undermining other African governments, yet supports UN intervention in the Congo and sanctions against South Africa.

traditional-family.rationale: Balewa's address to women delegates presents women's role in raising children and keeping the home and the moral fibre of the young as a stabilising force that even career women must honour.

unions-good.rationale: Balewa welcomed the amalgamation of Nigeria's small unions into a strong national trade union movement as a good sign for the country, while asking that wages rise with production.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nigeria kept the Queen as head of state at independence only as an interim arrangement, and Balewa's government made it a republic in October 1963 to reflect its sovereignty.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Balewa told Parliament in December 1962 that the government would very much like an effective opposition and a leader of the opposition, treating an opposing bench as part of parliamentary government.
